title: I See Your Diploma Signature and Raise You...
author: Matt Spivey
summary: Matt Spivey responds to a proposal by Hollis Robbins and Scott Latham that college presidents should personally certify that each graduate was genuinely examined and met departmental standards. He likes the idea but extends it to admissions: a president should also vouch, by signature, that every admitted student is qualified to do college work and was not accepted to meet a quota or enrolment target. He drafts a possible admissions certification and a right for professors to challenge admissions when students cannot read, write or do basic maths at college level. He then doubts any president would sign, drawing on his experience as a college athlete, coach and professor to describe coaches pressing admissions to accept recruits, and bonuses tied to enrolment growth. He closes that presidents care mostly about football, enrolment and contract renewals, so accountability is unlikely unless they stop prioritising revenue.
points: The proposal is to move presidential accountability to the front end of college, asking presidents to certify the competence of each admitted student as well as each graduate.
Spivey argues that grade inflation, AI and non-transferable grades have made diplomas weak signals of what graduates actually learned.
His insider account says athletic recruiting pressure and enrolment-linked bonuses encourage admissions staff to bend standards.
He allows that some presidents care about academics and would deserve recognition for taking on personal accountability.
The central obstacle he names is incentives: enrolment and the revenue it brings are often a president's primary concern.
quotes: With the value of degrees declining and trust in higher ed eroding, Robbins and Latham wonder, “What if college presidents had to publicly vouch for the degrees they hand out?

I love this idea, but I’d like to push it a step further: Shouldn’t a president be expected to vouch for the quality of every student being admitted to the school when the value of a degree and trust in higher ed is so low?

What if the president’s signature wasn’t just part of the conclusion of the education process, but also the beginning? To Robbins and Latham: I see your diploma signature and raise you an admissions letter signature.

Presidents largely care about three things: how the football team is doing, whether enrollment is up since last year, and when their contract is set to renew so they can negotiate a pay raise based on how “valuable” they are to the university.
As a former college athlete, coach, and professor, I can tell you that fudging acceptance metrics is a fairly regular occurrence.

It’s also common for staff and administrators to receive compensation bonuses for simply growing the numbers of enrollees, regardless of the academic or social consequences for the student body or potential harm to the university’s scholarly reputation.
Enrollment numbers and the revenue they drive are often a president’s primary concern. So, shoving dotted lines in front of them to sign is unlikely to motivate them.
